report:
**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by high-quality evidence.**

Abaloparatide, a synthetic analog of PTH-related protein and an anabolic bone-forming agent, has been shown to significantly reduce vertebral fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. The pivotal evidence comes from the **ACTIVE trial**, a phase 3 randomized controlled trial of 2,463 postmenopausal women, which found an **86% relative risk reduction** in new morphometric vertebral fractures with abaloparatide versus placebo over 18 months (0.58% vs. 4.22%; p < 0.001). Nonvertebral fractures were also reduced by 43% ([JAMA, Miller et al.](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2544640); [StatPearls, NIH](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK587447/)).

The **ACTIVExtend** extension study demonstrated that sequential abaloparatide followed by alendronate maintained fracture risk reduction, with an 84% relative reduction in vertebral fracture risk sustained over a longer follow-up ([Oxford Academic JBMR](https://academic.oup.com/jbmr/article/34/12/2213/7380871)).

A **systematic review and meta-analysis** confirmed that abaloparatide significantly reduced new vertebral fractures compared to placebo (p < 0.001) and improved bone mineral density at all skeletal sites ([MDPI JCM, 2026](https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/2/673)). A network meta-analysis further supported abaloparatide's efficacy for both vertebral and nonvertebral fracture reduction ([Springer, Osteoporosis International](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-019-04947-2)).

Based on these data, the FDA approved abaloparatide for postmenopausal women at high risk of fracture. The claim is accurate and strongly evidence-based.
